x.A: SCPs set the maximum permissions for accounts in an organization but don't grant permissions to individual users, so they can't give users access.
x.B: IAM roles can't be attached to groups. Groups get policies, and roles are assumed by principals.
x.C: A least-privilege IAM policy attached to the groups gives each department only the permissions it needs, and new users inherit them when they are added to a group.
x.D: Roles aren't associated with groups, and a permissions boundary only caps permissions without granting any.

x.A: s3:*Object on the bucket's objects would include GetObject, PutObject, and other object actions, which is more than the delete permission needed.
x.B: s3:* on the objects allows every S3 action, which is far more than needed and breaks least privilege.
x.C: The resource arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name* is a wildcard that would also match other buckets whose names start with bucket-name, so it is broader than necessary.
x.D: The policy already lets the group list the bucket, but s3:DeleteObject applies to objects, so it needs a statement for DeleteObject on arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/*. This adds only the missing permission.

x.A: Static website hosting with IAM read permissions doesn't make files public to everyone, and nothing prevents modification or deletion before the date.
x.B: A versioned bucket with Object Lock and a retention period until the date blocks changes and deletes until then, and static website hosting with a bucket policy makes the files publicly readable.
x.C: Restoring objects with Lambda after a change only reacts after the fact, and the original might already be altered or lost for a time.
x.D: Object Lock set on a folder isn't how it works, and read-only IAM permissions don't make the files public.

x.A: Systems Manager doesn't replicate and provision a whole infrastructure stack from a prototype.
x.B: Defining the infrastructure as a CloudFormation template and deploying it repeatably creates identical environments for development and production in two AZs, automatically.
x.C: AWS Config records resource configurations but can't deploy infrastructure.
x.D: Elastic Beanstalk can't take an existing manually built stack as a reference to deploy new environments.

x.A: KMS manages encryption keys and doesn't change the network path between EC2 and S3.
x.B: A VPC endpoint (a gateway endpoint for S3) keeps traffic between the EC2 instances and S3 on the AWS network, so it doesn't traverse the public internet.
x.C: A private subnet doesn't by itself give access to S3 without the internet. It would need a NAT or endpoint.
x.D: A virtual private gateway is used for VPN or Direct Connect to on-premises networks.

x.A: Lazy loading adds data to the cache only after a cache miss, so the cache can be missing or stale data right after a database write.
x.B: Write-through updates the cache every time data is written to the database, so the cache always matches the database.
x.C: Adding a TTL makes cached data expire after a time, but data can still be stale until it expires.
x.D: AppConfig is a configuration management feature and isn't a caching strategy.

x.A: The AWS CLI s3 sync command encrypts data in transit over HTTPS and takes no setup beyond the CLI. 100 GB over 100 Mbps takes only about 2 hours, so it has the least overhead.
x.B: DataSync works, but it needs an agent to deploy and manage, which is more overhead for 100 GB.
x.C: Snowball takes days to arrive and return, which is overkill for 100 GB over a 100 Mbps link.
x.D: A VPN adds setup and management work, and the CLI already encrypts in transit.

x.A: Lambda container images support Linux only, so a Windows container can't run on Lambda.
x.B: AWS Batch on Fargate doesn't support Windows containers.
x.C: ECS on Fargate supports Windows containers, and a scheduled task runs the job every 10 minutes. You pay only for the 1 to 3 minutes it runs each time.
x.D: Windows Task Scheduler inside a standalone task doesn't schedule tasks from outside the container, and it isn't how ECS schedules runs.

x.A: AWS Organizations with all features enabled lets you create many accounts centrally and apply governance such as SCPs and integration with IAM Identity Center.
x.B: Cognito identity pools are for app users, and IAM Identity Center doesn't accept Cognito authentication for workforce access.
x.C: SCPs limit permissions, and IAM Identity Center isn't added to Directory Service this way.
x.D: Organizations doesn't use Directory Service directly as its authentication mechanism.
x.E: IAM Identity Center integrated with the corporate directory gives users single sign-on access to all the accounts through the existing directory.

x.A: Glacier Flexible Retrieval with Expedited retrievals returns files in 1 to 5 minutes, so it meets the five minute requirement at a low storage cost for rarely restored footage.
x.B: Standard retrievals take 3 to 5 hours, which is longer than 5 minutes.
x.C: Standard-IA gives immediate access, but its storage price is much higher than Glacier for archives that are rarely restored.
x.D: One Zone-IA is also priced higher than Glacier and has less resilience, so it isn't the lowest cost for archives.

x.A: S3 hosts the static site cheaply, ECS on Fargate runs the containers without servers to manage, and RDS is a managed database. It simplifies deployment and reduces operational cost.
x.B: CloudFront is a CDN and doesn't host content by itself, and ECS on EC2 means managing the instances.
x.C: EKS on Fargate works but adds the EKS control plane charge and Kubernetes complexity, so it costs more and is more complex than ECS.
x.D: EC2 Reserved Instances for a static site and EKS on EC2 add servers and cluster management, so they're the most complex and costly.

x.A: FSx Multi-AZ deployments are Windows or other file systems but not the native NFS file system mountable from Linux instances both in AWS and on premises in the way EFS is, with no minimum size.
x.B: EBS Multi-Attach volumes attach only within one AZ to Nitro instances and can't be mounted from on premises.
x.C: EFS is a scalable, highly available NFS file system with no minimum size. Multiple mount targets across AZs let Linux instances in AWS and on-premises servers over the VPN mount it.
x.D: A single mount target is in one AZ, so it isn't highly available, and access points don't add availability.

x.A: The Billing managed policy gives access to billing, which is the opposite of the requirement.
x.B: An identity-based policy can't restrict the root user of a member account.
x.C: An SCP attached to the root OU denies access to billing information for all accounts, and SCPs apply to member account root users too.
x.D: Consolidated billing alone doesn't remove access to billing information, and it removes the features that SCPs need.

x.A: An SNS dead-letter queue can't target a Kinesis data stream, since only SQS queues are supported.
x.B: Putting an SQS queue between the application and SNS changes the architecture, and it won't retain messages that SNS failed to deliver to the endpoint.
x.C: An SNS dead-letter queue with an SQS target stores messages that SNS couldn't deliver to the subscribed HTTPS endpoint, and SQS retention can be set to 14 days for analysis. It takes almost no development.
x.D: DLQs for SNS support only SQS as a target, not DynamoDB.

x.A: An EMR cluster with a Hive job is a lot to set up and run, and it consumes read capacity from the table.
x.B: DynamoDB export to S3 uses point-in-time recovery and reads from the continuous backups, so it doesn't use the table's RCUs or affect availability, and needs no code.
x.C: A Lambda function consuming DynamoDB Streams requires code and only captures changes, not a full backup.
x.D: A Lambda export function takes code to write and reads from the table, which consumes RCUs.

x.A: A standard SQS queue as the Lambda event source gives at-least-once delivery at the lowest cost. SSE-KMS encrypts the messages, and the Lambda execution role needs kms:Decrypt to read them.
x.B: FIFO queues cost more and give exactly-once processing, which isn't needed. SSE-SQS isn't what the stated permission setup describes.
x.C: FIFO queues cost more than standard queues, and at-least-once processing doesn't require them.
x.D: The Lambda function itself doesn't get an encryption key invocation permission. The execution role needs kms:Decrypt.

x.A: Systems Manager templates only guide an approved process. Users can still create instances in other ways, so it doesn't restrict creation centrally.
x.B: Organizing the accounts into OUs and attaching an SCP that limits the allowed EC2 instance types centrally blocks oversized instances in all development accounts, with almost no development.
x.C: An EventBridge rule and Lambda that stop disallowed instances after they are created is custom code and lets instances start before being stopped.
x.D: Service Catalog works only if staff must use it, and you'd have to build and maintain the products, so it takes more effort than an SCP.

x.A: Comprehend analyzes text, such as sentiment, and doesn't translate audio recordings.
x.B: Lex builds conversational chatbots and doesn't create sentiment analysis reports.
x.C: Polly converts text to speech. It doesn't convert audio to text.
x.D: Transcribe converts speech to text and supports many languages, so recordings in any of the languages can be transcribed.
x.E: Translate translates text from many languages into English, which handles current and future languages.
x.F: Comprehend detects sentiment in text, so it produces the sentiment analysis reports, without the company maintaining ML models.

x.A: EC2 instances don't have resource-based policies that would produce this denial.
x.B: The policy is attached to a role, so an identity-based policy doesn't need a principal specified.
x.C: The first statement allows ec2:TerminateInstances on all resources, so the action is granted.
x.D: The second statement denies ec2:TerminateInstances unless the source IP is in 192.0.2.0/24 or 203.0.113.0/24. An explicit deny overrides the allow, so a request from another address gets a 403.

x.A: Audit Manager collects evidence for compliance frameworks and doesn't scan S3 data for PII.
x.B: S3 Inventory lists objects and metadata, not their contents, so it can't find PII.
x.C: Macie runs data discovery jobs on S3 buckets using managed data identifiers to find sensitive data such as passport numbers, credit card numbers, and other PII or financial information.
x.D: S3 Select retrieves a subset of data from a single object, so it can't classify sensitive data across a bucket.

x.A: S3 isn't a block or NFS file system and mounting it directly would require re-architecting the applications and gives no local caching.
x.B: A file gateway presents NFS shares backed by S3 with a local cache, so the NFS storage is replaced without changing the applications.
x.C: Snowball Edge is a temporary data transfer and edge compute device, not a permanent local caching storage solution.
x.D: A volume gateway provides iSCSI block storage with local caching backed by S3, which replaces the block storage without application changes.
x.E: EFS can be mounted from on premises only over Direct Connect or VPN and has no local caching.

x.A: A NAT instance in the public subnet still charges data processing through the instance and needs management, and it still sends S3 traffic over the internet path.

x.D: A second NAT gateway adds hourly charges and processes the same data, so costs go up.

x.A: An S3 Lifecycle rule can expire noncurrent versions and keep only a set number of newer noncurrent versions, so it keeps the two most recent versions automatically with no code.
x.B: A Lambda function to find and delete older versions means custom code to write and maintain.
x.C: S3 Batch Operations runs one-time jobs and isn't an ongoing, automatic cleanup, so it needs repeating.
x.D: Turning versioning off doesn't delete old versions, and it won't retain the two most recent versions.

x.A: A new 1 Gbps connection shared with another account still costs a full 1 Gbps port fee.
